title: wkexec input-delivery investigation: the 2026-07-23 correction chain (T3 ref)
desc: Dated archive for wkexec-conpty-keystrokes-ladder: the full sequence of wrong diagnoses and the measurements that killed each, ending at the delivery-channel ladder. Read before re-opening any input-delivery question.
steps: NAVIGATION: this is the FULL dated archive for the T1 core 'wkexec-conpty-keystrokes-ladder'. The core carries the current CONTRACT (flags, grammar, the delivery-channel ladder spec); everything below is the investigation history, kept because each entry records a diagnosis that looked right and was not. There is exactly ONE ref tier for this cluster -- add dated entries HERE, never open a second one, and never condense an entry away to make room (an earlier cluster orphaned a 34-step archive doing exactly that).

WRONG DIAGNOSIS 1 -- 'the child sees stdin EOF'. Evidence that seemed to support it: choice.exe printed its prompt then exited 255 in ~1.1s, with or without --keys; PowerShell Read-Host returned an empty string instead of blocking; powershell and cmd both exited in 1.3-1.9s unattended. A CRITICAL suggest was filed on this reading. What killed it: the same choice.exe failure reproduces with NO ConPTY at all, simply by redirecting stdout/stderr on a plain Start-Process, and choice works correctly in a real console (honours /T /D, rc=1). The 255 plus 'file is either empty or does not contain the valid choices' is what choice emits when its CONSOLE is unavailable -- it was never an EOF signal.

WRONG DIAGNOSIS 2 -- 'the child has no usable console'. Evidence: a P/Invoke probe reported GetConsoleMode, GetNumberOfConsoleInputEvents and GetConsoleScreenBufferInfo all failing with error 6 ERROR_INVALID_HANDLE inside the child. What killed it: the probe reported the SAME failures in its own control run on a known-good console, which means the instrument was broken, not the runtime. Ground truth measured afterwards with an absolute path: 'exec <abs>/cmd.exe /c "mode con"' prints 'Status for device CON: Lines 30, Columns 120' from inside the child -- the ConPTY is genuinely attached.

THE TWO CONFOUNDS that produced both wrong diagnoses, each of which silently changes WHAT IS BEING MEASURED while the command still looks correct. (1) MSYS PATH CONVERSION: from Git-Bash, '/c' is rewritten to 'C:/' before wkappbot ever sees the argument, so the run tests a different command than the one typed -- MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 is mandatory for any Windows-style switch. (2) SHIM HIJACK: a BARE target name resolves to a repo shim -- 'exec cmd' ran bin/cmd.CMD through the ad-hoc launch path, never touching ConPTY, and produced empty output with rc=0 that read as 'no console'. ALWAYS use an absolute target path when measuring exec.

REAL BUG FOUND 1 -- ARGUMENT LEAKAGE. exec's own value-taking flags were not stripped from the CHILD command line: BuildExecChildArgs listed only the OLD spellings, so after the --keys/--onexit/--reply/--noise rename, 'exec choice.exe /C YN --keys f' handed '--keys f' to choice.exe as bogus choices. The launch banner exposed it verbatim by printing the child's exact command line. powershell had hidden it for weeks because it ignores surplus arguments. Fixed with a single ExecOwnValueFlags table holding both spellings, so a future flag cannot be forgotten.

REAL BUG FOUND 2 -- THE INJECTION LOG WAS LYING. The stdin-inject callback was 'try { WriteFile(...); } catch { }' with the return value ignored, while the caller unconditionally printed '[EXEC:PTY] Injected N bytes'. A failed or short write was indistinguishable from a delivered one, and every diagnosis above was built on top of that lie. Replaced with a checked write that logs err + byte count + handle on failure, short-write counts, and a thrown exception instead of discarding it. IMMEDIATE PAYOFF: with the check in place the write was shown to SUCCEED, which is what narrowed the defect to the child not reading the pipe we write to.

THE STATE AT HANDOFF: ConPTY attachment is healthy (mode con proves it), the injection write succeeds (checked write proves it), and yet the child behaves as though its stdin is at EOF from the first instant -- 'cmd /v:on /c "set /p X=P: && echo GOT-!X!"' prints its prompt and returns rc=1 immediately, injecting 4 seconds after the child is up changes nothing, and CR versus LF makes no difference. Piping data into the PARENT's stdin does not reach the child either. So the bytes enter a pipe nobody reads.

THE FINDING THAT REFRAMED EVERYTHING: wkstdpty.ps1 -- cited across this cluster as the working interactive driver -- contains NO CreatePseudoConsole. It sets psi.RedirectStandardInput on an ordinary Process and writes to p.StandardInput. So a ConPTY input path has NEVER been demonstrated to deliver a byte in this codebase; what IS proven is the plain redirected pipe. Re-reading the agy evidence accordingly: the 99 test's prompt arrived via the '-i <prompt>' COMMAND-LINE argument, and the '/quit' that was supposed to arrive via the keystrokes file is precisely the thing that never worked (the C5 clean-exit criterion hung until KillAfterMs every run). Every apparent keystroke success is explained without ConPTY input ever delivering anything.

METHOD LESSONS worth more than the bug: measure the INSTRUMENT before the patient (a probe that fails on a known-good control is broken, not evidence); a control run captured through the same plumbing as the patient is not a control; prefer a datum the mechanism EMITS about itself (the launch banner printing the child's command line is what finally exposed the real bug) over an outcome you interpret; and when every execution path you control is already redirected, say so and ask the human for the one uncontrolled run rather than inferring -- a single command typed by the user in a real terminal ended three rounds of wrong answers.

SECTOR-A FINDING 2026-07-24, VALUABLE BUT MIS-ATTRIBUTED -- a real hazard proven, the observed stall NOT explained. A commando diagnosing why --reply stalls the relay built two C# provers under .tmp/reply-diag/ and demonstrated CATASTROPHIC REGEX BACKTRACKING: the pattern [a-z]+([a-z]+)*:[a-z]* against 1000 a-characters plus a non-matching tail hung for over 15 seconds, and a 6-pattern sweep timed out at 120s. The mechanism is textbook and the hazard is REAL: RunCommand.Pty.OnMatch.cs calls rule.CompiledRegex.Match with NO timeout, on the stdout relay thread, so any pathological caller pattern wedges the entire relay -- which is exactly why no output appears rather than merely no rule firing. WORTH FIXING regardless: pass a match timeout, and consider rejecting nested quantifiers at parse time. BUT IT IS NOT THE CAUSE OF THE REPORTED BUG. The patterns that actually hung in the live runs were ASKNOW and P: -- literal strings with no quantifier at all, nested or otherwise, which cannot backtrack. The commando constructed its own pathological input and proved a mechanism instead of testing the pattern that failed. That is the same substitution shape seen three other times in this session: when the required evidence cannot be produced, the nearest producible artifact is offered in its place, honestly and unprompted, and it looks like a result. REFLEX for the reviewer: when a diagnosis names a mechanism, check that the mechanism's PRECONDITION was present in the failing case -- here, ask whether the failing pattern could backtrack at all. If the precondition is absent, the finding may still be a genuine bug worth filing, but the original defect remains OPEN and must not be closed on it. STILL OPEN: why a literal-pattern --reply produces zero relay output. Next probe should instrument the relay loop itself rather than the regex.

T1-vs-T2 COMPARISON RESULT (2026-07-23, the decisive experiment): same target, same input, only the channel differs. T1 PLAIN PIPE -- an ordinary Process with RedirectStandardInput, writing 'y\r\n' to StandardInput then closing it -- DELIVERS: 'cmd /v:on /c "set /p X=P: && echo GOT-!X!"' returns rc=0 and prints GOT-y. T2 ConPTY, the path exec currently takes, does NOT deliver: the same target prints its prompt and returns rc=1 without ever receiving the byte, and this holds with --keys, with late injection 4s after the child is up, and with CR instead of LF. VERDICT: the delivery-channel ladder spec is confirmed by measurement -- plain redirected stdin is the rung that works and must be FIRST-CLASS, not a pre-Win10 fallback beneath ConPTY. IMPLEMENTATION GOTCHA found in the same run: the T1 output was 'GOT-<BOM>y' -- a UTF-8 byte-order mark preceded the payload because .NET's StandardInput StreamWriter defaults to an encoding that emits a preamble. A target parsing a single keypress or a strict token will choke on that invisible prefix. When wiring T1, write RAW BYTES or construct the writer with new UTF8Encoding(false); never trust the default. This is the same class of defect as the CR-vs-LF question: the byte on the wire is what matters, so dump it and look.

TODO: 2026-07-24 (user directive, SPEC) SPLIT THE FIX SURFACE OUT OF RunCommand.Pty.OnMatch.cs -- and note this is already STANDING PRACTICE, not a new idea. wksplit-cs-utility step 21 makes extract-before-you-edit a standing mandatory practice for any shared source, and step 23 makes it a REQUIRED LINE IN EVERY SOURCE-EDIT AGENT BRIEF, with a subfolder rule: when the target folder already holds many files, nest the split-out parts under a subfolder named after the original source, so Commands/ does not explode with siblings. This session re-derived the same conclusion from scratch without reading it -- the third time today a documented answer was rediscovered the expensive way. RECONCILING the two orderings: extract FIRST as the standard says, and let the diagnosis choose only the SEAM. The file crossed 438 lines and auto-acquired a wksplit-400 study-lock, so the whole file is now gated for any edit, while the actual repair surface is a few dozen lines: the scan-and-fire loop and the injection call inside it. Splitting narrows both the lock and the review to the lines that change. WHY ORDER MATTERS: the natural seam is the one the bug reveals -- if the FD sector confirms the fire path blocks the relay, the boundary is exactly SCAN-AND-DECIDE versus INJECT-AND-RECORD, and the split falls out of the diagnosis for free. Cutting first means guessing the seam, and a wrong seam is worse than no split: it scatters the repair across two files and leaves a partial-class join nobody can follow. PROPOSED SEAM, to confirm against the finding: keep pattern parsing, ANSI stripping, noise application, rolling-window management and match resolution in the current file, and move the FIRE half -- the write to the child's stdin, the fire log line, the debounce update and the cap accounting -- into RunCommand.Pty.OnMatch.Fire.cs. That half is what is suspected of blocking, what needs a timeout or a non-blocking write, and what a reviewer must read closely. FOLLOW THE DOCUMENTED SPLIT PROCEDURE, not an ad-hoc cut: wksplit-cs-utility for the six safety gates, and the round-trip symbol-set check so nothing is silently dropped -- a cheap split once lost roughly 320 lines that still compiled. Register the new file's harness:skill lock in the same commit, or the new half ships unguarded.

FD SECTOR 2026-07-24: verdict CONFIRMED, but its own numbers REFUTE it -- and the refutation is the useful part. The report claimed the fire path blocks the relay when a rule matches and the child never reads stdin. Its evidence: matching rule 2604ms with output and a clean exit, non-matching rule 2731ms with output and a clean exit. The two cases are indistinguishable, so matching is not the discriminator and nothing was confirmed. The reported defect was an INDEFINITE hang with ZERO output, killed at 30s -- a 2.6s run that produced output is a different phenomenon entirely. WHAT THE DATA ACTUALLY SHOWS, and it inverts the hypothesis: children that do NOT read stdin (echo) complete fine, while children that DO read stdin (Read-Host, set /p) hang. So the failure is not a blocking write wedging the relay -- it is that the injected bytes never REACH a child that is waiting for them. That points at the same root as the exec capture defect filed the same day, where PTY output does not reach an inherited handle: an input-side counterpart of a handle-plumbing problem, not a threading one. TWO GENUINE FINDINGS SURVIVE. (1) PipeInput.cs line 79 does perform a BLOCKING stdin write under a lock FROM the stdout relay thread -- unexercised so far, but a real hazard that should be made timeout-bounded or moved off the relay thread before it bites. (2) outTask.Wait(2000) imposes a FIXED two-second cost on every run regardless of rules, which the timing above exposes and which nobody had noticed. REVIEWER REFLEX, the sixth instance of this shape in one session: when a report says CONFIRMED, read its NUMBERS before its conclusion -- here both arms of the experiment matched, which is the signature of a hypothesis that was not tested rather than one that was proven.

AG SECTOR 2026-07-24, ACCEPTED -- and it corrects the previous step's theory. This report finally supplied PRESENCE evidence rather than a launcher artifact: it quoted agy's own output (Antigravity CLI 1.1.5, the account line, Gemini 3.1 Pro, the generated reply Hello I am here and read, and a 273-token counter), which is exactly what an earlier sector failed to do when it offered the launcher's foreground-window-title field as proof that agy had responded. It also proved that an injected ESC REACHES agy and is processed. THAT INVERTS THE PRIOR CONCLUSION: injection is not universally failing to arrive. The boundary is the child's READ MODE. A raw-console TUI reader like agy receives injected keys fine. A stream or line reader like PowerShell Read-Host or cmd set /p does not, and hangs waiting. This is precisely the T1-pipe versus T2-console split the delivery-channel ladder predicted, now confirmed from the other direction: the same injection path serves one class and not the other, which is why a single transport can never cover both and the ladder must choose per target. WHAT REMAINS UNPROVEN: termination. The current exit sequence still hangs to timeout because agy's native permission prompt accepts only its numeric options, so the trailing quit is ignored. The sector prepared but did NOT run the fix -- answering the menu numerically BEFORE quitting -- and said so plainly rather than claiming success, which is the correct handoff. Test sequences and the change site (line 14 of wkexec-agy.ps1) are in .tmp/wkexec-agy-proof/RETRY.md. NOTE the sequence itself is a termination fix, not a whitelist, and weakens no harness assertion.
